script.opening: "I had COVID about four months ago and I’m just not right. I’m exhausted all the time, breathless going upstairs, my brain’s foggy and I can’t concentrate at work, and whenever I try to do more I crash badly for days. People think I should be over it. Is this in my head?"

facts.text: Since COVID in June (positive home test, a week in bed, not admitted). Exhausted all the time. Breathless on stairs — not getting worse. Can’t find words, loses her thread in meetings. Heart sometimes races when she stands up.

If she does more — a long day at work, a walk with friends — she is "wiped out" the next day for 2–3 days, with aches and flu-like feeling. Has been trying to "push through" and exercise more, as a friend advised.

No chest pain, no coughing blood, no calf swelling, no fainting. Breathless only on exertion, not at rest or lying flat. No weight loss, no night sweats, no fevers. Periods normal, not heavy. No thirst or passing urine more.

If asked: "The practice nurse saw me last week — she said my oxygen was 98%, blood pressure fine, and when she did a standing-up test my pulse went up by about 25 but my blood pressure didn’t drop." No blood tests yet.
"Fed up and worried. Not depressed, I don’t think." Sleep broken. No thoughts of self-harm.
Primary school deputy head. Back at work full time for 6 weeks, "barely surviving"; spends weekends in bed. Single mum to a 12-year-old son. Health: no medicines, no allergies, non-smoker.

Articulate, tired, slightly defensive — expect not to be believed. Relief if the doctor validates it. Surprised to be told to pace rather than push: "That’s the opposite of what I’ve been doing." Dreads telling work she needs adjustments.

ice.ideas: "People at work think I should be over it. I’m starting to wonder if it’s in my head."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of losing her job and of letting her son down; worried something serious like heart damage is being missed.
ice.expectations: "To manage a full day at work without paying for it. And someone to take it seriously."

checkpoints.text: Recognises and VALIDATES POST-COVID SYNDROME (symptoms >12 weeks after COVID-19, not otherwise explained; fatigue, breathlessness, brain fog, post-exertional malaise) as a real condition

EXCLUDES alternative/serious causes and red flags — breathlessness/chest pain (PE, cardiac, pneumonia), fatigue causes (anaemia, thyroid, diabetes) — using the recorded sats, lying and standing pulse/BP and sit-to-stand, arranging a face-to-face chest/heart examination, NICE NG188 bloods (including CRP, BNP, HbA1c), ECG and chest X-ray by 12 weeks, rather than attributing all to long COVID
Assesses HOLISTICALLY across physical, cognitive, psychological and functional domains, screening mood and understanding the post-exertional pattern

Manages with PACING/energy conservation (avoiding boom-and-bust and not advising pushing through or fixed incremental graded exercise, NICE NG206 principles), symptom-specific management, and refers to a long-COVID/rehabilitation service
Supports FUNCTION and return to work (phased/adjustments, fit note, Equality Act 2010) and sets realistic, fluctuating-recovery expectations
VALIDATES the experience (not "in your head"), counters the sense of being disbelieved, and checks understanding without dismissiveness
Explores the impact on her work, home and sense of self and what recovery would mean to her, and builds the rehabilitation plan around her own goals and priorities

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting urgent assessment, results of basic investigations, pacing/rehabilitation plan, work support, referral, and review — validation + exclusion + rehabilitation, not dismissal

worked.txt: "First — this is not in your head. What you’re describing is post-COVID syndrome, or long COVID: real, recognised symptoms that can persist for months. I’m glad you came, and I believe you."

"That said, I won’t just blame everything on COVID — your breathlessness deserves checking, the nurse’s checks last week were reassuring — your oxygen stayed normal after the sit-to-stand, though your pulse rose when you stood up — and I’d like you in to listen to your chest and heart, with a heart tracing, a chest X-ray and some bloods (count, iron, kidneys, liver, thyroid, sugar, inflammation and a heart marker) to rule out other causes."

"Let’s look at all of it — the energy, the breathing, the brain fog, your mood, and how it’s affecting work and daily life. The crashing after activity is an important pattern that changes how we approach this."

"Because you crash when you push, the key is pacing — working within your energy envelope, doing a bit less than you can, spreading activity with rests, and only increasing slowly when you’re stable, rather than boom-and-bust or a fixed exercise programme. I’ll show you how, and there’s a long-COVID rehab service I’ll refer you to."

"Let’s sort work too — a phased return or adjustments, and a fit note if you need one. If it goes on, your employer may have to make reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act. Recovery can be slow and up-and-down, and that’s normal."

"Come back urgently or call 999 if your breathlessness suddenly worsens, you get chest pain, cough up blood, faint, or have palpitations with feeling faint — those need checking promptly. Otherwise we’ll review your results and your progress together."

f.learning: POST-COVID SYNDROME (long COVID) is symptoms continuing or developing more than 12 weeks after acute COVID-19 and not explained by an alternative diagnosis — commonly profound fatigue, breathlessness, "brain fog"/cognitive impairment, palpitations, chest tightness, sleep disturbance, and POST-EXERTIONAL malaise (crashing after activity) — and the first step is to recognise and VALIDATE it as a real, recognised condition, countering the patient’s fear that it is "in their head". Critically, do NOT attribute everything to long COVID without EXCLUDING alternative/serious causes and red flags: new or worsening breathlessness or chest pain should prompt exclusion of PE, cardiac disease and pneumonia, and fatigue should prompt basics per NICE NG188 (FBC, renal and liver function, CRP, ferritin, BNP, HbA1c, thyroid), with sats, an exercise-tolerance test such as a 1-minute sit-to-stand and lying and standing pulse and BP (which a practice nurse can record), a face-to-face chest and heart examination, an ECG, and a chest X-ray by 12 weeks if respiratory symptoms continue; refer urgently for hypoxaemia, desaturation on exercise, severe lung disease or cardiac chest pain, and consider PE (NICE NG158). Assess holistically across physical, cognitive, psychological and functional domains, screen mood, and understand the post-exertional pattern, which shapes management. Manage with supportive REHABILITATION centred on PACING/energy conservation (avoiding boom-and-bust, especially with post-exertional malaise — no pushing through and no fixed incremental graded exercise, NICE NG206 principles), symptom-specific management, sleep and breathing techniques, and psychological support, referring to a long-COVID/post-COVID rehabilitation service where available. Support function and return to work (phased return/adjustments, fit note, Equality Act 2010 reasonable adjustments), validate the experience and avoid dismissiveness, set realistic expectations of slow and fluctuating recovery, and safety-net for red flags.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG188 COVID-19 rapid guideline: managing the long-term effects of COVID-19 · [2] NICE NG206 Myalgic encephalomyelitis (or encephalopathy)/chronic fatigue syndrome · [3] NICE NG158 Venous thromboembolic diseases · [4] DWP: fit note guidance · [5] Equality Act 2010
knowledge.summary: Symptoms continuing more than 12 weeks after acute COVID-19 and not explained by another diagnosis are post-COVID-19 syndrome [1]. Believe her, exclude other causes with targeted tests and examination (recorded observations, a sit-to-stand test on video, and an in-person examination where needed), refer urgently if red flags, and support self-management with pacing, rehabilitation referral and work adjustments.

points.t: Ongoing symptomatic COVID-19: 4 to 12 weeks. Post-COVID-19 syndrome: over 12 weeks, not explained by an alternative diagnosis. Symptoms often overlap, fluctuate and change [1].

Holistic history: symptoms, their pattern and impact, and mood. Examination including oxygen saturation, pulse, BP and chest (recorded by a clinician or with home equipment; arrange an in-person chest examination if needed). Exercise tolerance suited to the person (for example a 1-minute sit-to-stand test with pulse and saturation), and lying and standing pulse and BP if postural symptoms [1].

Bloods guided by symptoms, such as FBC, renal and liver function, CRP, ferritin, BNP, HbA1c and thyroid function. Chest X-ray by 12 weeks if respiratory symptoms continue. ECG with palpitations or chest pain [1].

Severe hypoxaemia or oxygen desaturation on exercise, signs of severe lung disease, cardiac chest pain [1]. Consider pulmonary embolism with new pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or sudden breathlessness (NICE NG158) [3].

Self-management support, including pacing and setting realistic goals, and referral to an integrated multidisciplinary assessment service after other causes are excluded; referral can be from 4 weeks [1]. Where post-exertional symptom exacerbation occurs, do not advise pushing through, and do not offer fixed incremental graded exercise (NICE NG206 principles for ME/CFS) [2].

Fit note with adjustments such as a phased return or altered hours [4]. Long-lasting symptoms with a substantial effect on daily activity may meet the Equality Act 2010 definition of disability, which requires reasonable adjustments [5].
Screen for anxiety and depression and offer support; psychological symptoms do not mean the illness is “in her head”.

model.text: Hello Ms Whitfield, I’m Dr O’Neill. What brings you in?

I had COVID about four months ago and I’m just not right. I’m exhausted all the time, breathless going upstairs, my brain’s foggy and I can’t concentrate at work, and whenever I try to do more I crash badly for days. People think I should be over it. Is this in my head?
I can hear how much this is affecting you, and I believe you. What you’re describing is real, and we see it after COVID. Let me ask more so we can make sure nothing else is going on.
Tell me about the breathlessness. Is it only on exertion, and has it changed recently? Any chest pain, coughing blood, or leg swelling?
model.why: Red flags for cardiac, PE and lung disease

model.text: Stairs mainly. It’s not getting worse. No chest pain, no blood.
Any heart racing or thumping, and does it happen when you stand up? Any fainting?
Sometimes my heart races. I haven’t fainted.
When you crash after doing more, how long after, and how long does it last?
Usually the next day, then I’m wiped out for days.
How’s your sleep, appetite, and weight? Any fevers or night sweats?
Sleep’s broken. Nothing else like that.
And how has your mood been through all this?
Fed up and worried. Not depressed, I don’t think.
You asked if it’s in your head. Where has that worry come from?
People at work think I should be over it. I’m starting to wonder myself.
What would getting better look like for you, and what were you hoping for today?
To manage a full day at work without paying for it. And someone to take it seriously.

The nurse’s checks last week are in your notes — your oxygen level at rest and after a one-minute sit-to-stand, and your pulse and blood pressure lying and standing. (Recorded: no desaturation on exertion; pulse rises from 74 to 99 on standing without a fall in blood pressure; no red flags.)
model.why: NICE NG188 recorded examination and exercise test

model.text: Nothing I’ve found needs emergency treatment. I’d also like blood tests: blood count, iron stores, kidneys, liver, thyroid, sugar, inflammation and a heart marker. And a heart tracing because of the racing, and a chest X-ray because the breathlessness has lasted this long.
model.why: Targeted tests to exclude other causes (NICE NG188)

model.text: So you do think something could be wrong?

I think this is most likely long COVID, which is what we call symptoms lasting over 12 weeks. The tests are to make sure we’re not missing anything that’s easier to treat, like anaemia or a thyroid problem. It isn’t in your head.
model.why: Names post-COVID-19 syndrome; explains the purpose of tests

model.text: The crashing matters. Pushing through tends to make it worse. The approach is pacing: working out how much you can do without crashing, doing a bit less than that, and spreading activity through the day with rests. We only increase slowly when you’re stable.
That’s the opposite of what I’ve been doing.
Most people do the same. I’d also like to refer you to the local long COVID service, which has physios, occupational therapists and psychologists.
And work?

We can do a fit note saying you may be fit for work with adjustments, such as a phased return, fewer hours or flexible breaks. If it goes on, your employer may have to make reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act. Would that help?
Yes. I’ve been dreading telling them.
We can word it so it’s clear. Which bit of the plan feels most doable this week?
Planning rests at work, I think.

If you get sudden or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, fainting or a racing heart with dizziness, get seen urgently or call 999. I’ll see you with the results in two weeks. What will you tell work?
That I’ve got long COVID, I’m having tests, and I need a phased return with rests.
Perfect. And thank you for coming. You did the right thing.

pitfalls.intro: The station rewards belief plus rigour. Candidates fail by dismissing her, by blaming everything on COVID without tests, and by advising her to push through.

items.why: Her main fear is being disbelieved.
items.fix: Answer “is it in my head?” directly and early.

items.why: NICE NG188 requires excluding other causes and checking for red flags.
items.fix: Sats, lying and standing BP, sit-to-stand, bloods, ECG, chest X-ray.

items.fail: Advising graded exercise or pushing through.
items.why: Post-exertional crashing worsens with it (NICE NG206 principles).

items.fail: Missing PE or cardiac red flags.
items.why: Breathlessness and palpitations have serious causes (NICE NG158).
items.fix: Ask about chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, sudden change.

items.why: Work is her main functional goal.
items.fix: Fit note with adjustments; Equality Act.

items.why: Results and a fluctuating course need review.
items.fix: Book a results review and name the red flags.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your energy like a phone battery that’s lost capacity since COVID. If you run it to zero, it takes days to recharge. Pacing means stopping before it runs out.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered if it was in your head. It isn’t. What you describe is a recognised condition.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around her goal of a full working day; support conversations with her employer.
sharedPlan: Recorded examination and sit-to-stand test; tests per NICE NG188 (bloods, ECG, chest X-ray)
Pacing without pushing through; referral to the long COVID service
Fit note with a phased return or adjustments; Equality Act reasonable adjustments
safetyNet: Sudden or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, fainting or a racing heart with dizziness: urgent assessment or 999
Review with results in two weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The station rewards belief plus rigour. Candidates fail by dismissing her, by blaming everything on COVID without tests, and by advising her to push through.

items.why: Her main fear is being disbelieved.
items.fix: Answer “is it in my head?” directly and early.

items.why: NICE NG188 requires excluding other causes and checking for red flags.
items.fix: Sats, lying and standing BP, sit-to-stand, bloods, ECG, chest X-ray.

items.fail: Advising graded exercise or pushing through.
items.why: Post-exertional crashing worsens with it (NICE NG206 principles).

items.fail: Missing PE or cardiac red flags.
items.why: Breathlessness and palpitations have serious causes (NICE NG158).
items.fix: Ask about chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, sudden change.

items.why: Work is her main functional goal.
items.fix: Fit note with adjustments; Equality Act.

items.why: Results and a fluctuating course need review.
items.fix: Book a results review and name the red flags.
